phonemes.desc: Short iota — the 'ee' of 'see', lightly sounded.
Phi, the aspirated p of classical Greek — 'p' released with a breath of air, as in 'uphill' said quickly.
Gamma-epsilon with the Greek acute: the stressed syllable, and a hard 'g' as in 'go'.
Nu-epsilon-iota in hiatus — two short vowels, 'neh-ee', not a diphthong.

pronunciation.approximation: ee-fee-GEH-neh-ee-ah — five syllables, the classical p aspirated, the g hard as in 'go'; the Greek acute falls on GE.

kin.label: Root
kin.form: γένος (génos), 'birth, race, kind' — cognate with Latin genus and English 'kin' (PIE *ǵenh₁-).

kin.label: Debatable element
kin.form: ἶφι (ĩphi), 'by might, force' — of uncertain origin; Beekes judges it possibly Pre-Greek, and the old comparison with Sanskrit īś- 'to have power' is insecure.

kin.label: Epic doublet
kin.form: Iphianassa (Ἰφιάνασσα) — the name Homer gives (Iliad 9.145, 287) to Agamemnon's daughter, long identified with Iphigéneia.

pronunciation.note: Iphigéneia is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the acute accent preserves the inherited Greek stress, but every vowel in Ἰφιγένεια is short — the antepenult accent itself proves the ultima is light. Nothing further distinguishes the name from its ASCII form.

domains.title: Iphigeneia
domains.subtitle: Sacrifice
domains.lead: Iphigéneia is sacrifice, winds, aulis. The name means "Mighty-born" — ἶφι, "by might," joined to γένος, "birth, race" — and hers is the Greek tradition's most searching account of what the Trojan War cost before it ever reached Troy.

cards.name: Sacred Name
cards.desc: The restoration Iphigéneia returns the acute of Ἰφιγένεια and the name's full weight: "Mighty-born," the girl who carried her fate in her name.

cards.name: Sacrifice
cards.desc: Summoned to Aulis on the pretext of marriage to Achilles, she became the price of the wind that would carry a thousand ships to Troy (Euripides, Iphigenia at Aulis).

cards.name: Living Tradition
cards.desc: Priestess of Artemis among the Taurians, then guardian of girls' passage at Brauron, where Athens showed her tomb (Euripides, Iphigenia in Tauris; Pausanias 1.33.1).

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Preserved as a flagship temple despite the unregistrable plain-ASCII form.

symbols.name: The saffron robe
symbols.meaning: The garment that poured to the ground at the altar (Aeschylus, Agamemnon 239) — maidenhood offered up in fabric.

symbols.name: The deer
symbols.meaning: The substitute Artemis set on the altar in the Cypria's version — the rescue the epic grants her, taken back as suddenly as given.

symbols.name: The letter
symbols.meaning: The written word that reunited her with Orestes in the Tauris — recognition carried by text, not tokens or scars.

symbols.name: The bear (arktos)
symbols.meaning: The little girls who served Artemis Brauronia before marriage — Iphigéneia's Athenian afterlife as guardian of the passage she never lived.

symbols.name: The becalmed sea
symbols.meaning: Aulis's windless harbor — the fleet's stillness ended only at her altar.

mythology.lead: Iphigéneia's story is the price of the Trojan War paid in advance: the maiden summoned to Aulis as a bride, lifted over her father's altar as the fleet's ransom, and — in the tellings that spare her — swept to the far shore of the Black Sea, where the gods set her a second altar and made her its keeper.

myths.title: The Fleet That Would Not Sail
myths.text:
The Cypria, the lost epic of the war's beginnings, told it first: the Greek fleet gathers at Aulis and the winds die. Agamemnon has angered Artemis — in the epic's account by killing a stag in the goddess's grove and boasting he could outshoot her. The seer Kalkhas announces the price: the fleet will sail only when the king gives his daughter Iphigéneia to the goddess. Aeschylus compresses the whole unbearable machinery into the parodos of the Agamemnon (104–257): the portent of two eagles tearing a hare — 'sacrifice a suffering thing' — and the elder king, 'clothed in ruinous frenzy', willing the act with 'a wretched holiness'.

What the tradition insists on is not the savagery but the logic: the war against Troy begins by consuming the Greeks' own, at home, before a single ship clears the harbor. Ten years of foreign slaughter are inaugurated by one deliberate domestic one.

myths.title: The Deer on the Altar
myths.text:
Aeschylus stages what the epic only reported, and makes it the most harrowing scene in surviving Greek poetry (Agamemnon 228–247): the girl, 'gagged like a goat', lifted over the altar by her father's men; 'her saffron robe pouring to the ground'; one glance, one cry for her brother — and her father, 'after that decision, willed it', 'and so the ships sailed'. The Cypria softened the blow for its audiences: Artemis snatched the maiden from the altar, set a deer in her place, and carried Iphigéneia to the land of the Taurians, where she made her immortal.

Euripides, in Iphigenia at Aulis, splits the difference and finds the truth inside the contradiction: his Iphigéneia arrives deceived — promised to Achilles — and then, at the last, chooses the sacrifice herself, declaring her death shall be Greece's freedom. The tradition never lets us settle whether she was murdered, rescued, or volunteered; the ambiguity is the point, because all three answers say the same thing about war's arithmetic.

myths.title: Priestess of the Strangers
myths.text:
Euripides' Iphigenia in Tauris finds her years later on the northern Black Sea coast — the Crimean Chersonesos of later geography — priestess of a savage Artemis whose rite demands that any Greek cast ashore be consecrated and slaughtered at the altar. She has become, in her own bitter office, the one who prepares the victims. Her opening monologue is the tradition's most direct audit of the Aulis bargain: she was sacrificed, she says, so that Helen might be recovered and the Greeks might go free — and the brother she died for now stands, in her dream, dead by her own hand at that very altar.

The myth's cruelty is precise: the rescued girl is installed as executioner of her own people. Survival, the play suggests, is not the opposite of sacrifice but its continuation — the gods saved her body and spent her life.

myths.title: The Letter and the Statue
myths.text:
The escape fills the second half of the Iphigenia in Tauris: two Greek captives are brought in, and one is Orestés, sent by Apollo to steal the Taurian image of Artemis. Recognition comes by letter — the play's celebrated scene of Orestés refusing to believe the impossible, and Iphigéneia inventing on the spot the fiction of a ritual purification to save them both. They seize the goddess's statue, flee to the ship, and are caught in the shallows until Athēnâ intervenes, commanding that the image be given a new home at Halai in Attica and that the goddess receive a rite in which a sword is drawn at a man's throat in token, bloodlessly — 'so shall the goddess have her honors'. King Thoas, cheated of his victims, accepts the goddess's will with one of tragedy's most humane exits: if gods they are, they are beyond his vengeance.

The ending converts a cult of human sacrifice into a festival of symbolic remembrance — myth rewriting ritual into mercy, and an audience taught to prefer it.

myths.title: The Bears of Brauron
myths.text:
The Athenians gave her a home and a function. At Brauron on Attica's east coast stood the sanctuary of Artemis Brauronia, where girls — the famous arktoi, 'bears' — served the goddess before marriage, dancing in saffron robes and dedicating their childhood garments on leaving (Aristophanes, Lysistrata 641–647; the rite's sacred law survives inscribed on marble). Pausanias (1.33.1) saw Iphigéneia's tomb and cult there, and the clothes of women who had died in childbirth dedicated at her shrine; Megara disputed the honor with a rival tomb of its own (Pausanias 1.43.1). Later antiquity multiplied her endings: Antoninus Liberalis (27), after Nikander, reports that Artemis made her immortal as Hekátē; and the tragedians preserve the strangest variant — that she was not Agamemnon's daughter at all but Theseus' child by Helen (Stesichorus; Euripides, Iphigenia at Aulis 509–512), born of a kidnapping before the war ever had a cause.

Whichever ending a city preferred, the office is constant: the maiden sacrificed to launch a war becomes the guardian of every girl's passage into adult life.

lore.syncretism: Greek tradition quietly merged two figures: the Iliad (9.145, 287) knows Agamemnon's daughter only as Iphianassa, and the cyclic tradition's Iphigéneia was long read as the same girl under an older name. Antoninus Liberalis (27), following Nikander, reports her final promotion: Artemis made her immortal as Hekátē — a striking equation, since both receive offerings at liminal places and both govern the marginal. Roman poets kept the Aulis scene central: Lucretius (De Rerum Natura 1.84–101) names her 'the maiden of Trivia' and sets the sacrificial fillet among religion's cruelties, while Ovid (Metamorphoses 12.24–38) repeats the stag substitution in his roll-call of the war's causes. Later antiquity fixed her geography, identifying the Taurian temple with the Chersonesos in Crimea — the identification still printed beside maps of the myth.
lore.culturalLegacy: Iphigéneia's afterlife is a one-woman argument across Western art. Euripides left a matched pair — the Iphigenia at Aulis, where she consents to die, and the Iphigenia in Tauris, where she refuses to kill — and every age has staged the two against each other. Racine's Iphigénie (1674) made her the tragedy of state reason; Gluck's operas Iphigénie en Aulide (1774) and en Tauride (1779) gave her the century's most humane music; Goethe's Iphigenie auf Tauris (1787) rewrote the escape as the triumph of pure humanity over custom — 'when humans help themselves, the gods are well disposed.' Her name survives in scholarship as the archetype of the sacrificed child, invoked wherever a society's great project demands a small victim. The cult memory is real too: Brauron's sanctuary still stands, and the arkteia it served remains a cornerstone of what we know about Greek girls' lives.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Iphigéneia asks the question Greek tragedy never stops asking: what kind of necessity can require the death of a child, and who is responsible for obeying it? The tradition refuses a clean answer three times over. In the epic, the gods demand it and the father consents. In Euripides' Aulis, the victim consents too — and her consent, freely given for a nation's freedom, disturbs us more than any command could. In the Tauris, the one who was spared is ordered to become the executioner, and the play's mercy lies in her refusal.

The myth is the West's earliest study of sunk-cost devotion: a fleet assembled, a cause declared, an altar built — and each step making the sacrifice harder to undo. What Iphigéneia finally teaches is not that sacrifice is wicked but that it is always a choice wearing necessity's clothing, and the person on the altar sees the clothing most clearly of all.
lore.archaeology: The material record belongs to her cult, not her story. The sanctuary of Artemis at Brauron in eastern Attica, excavated by the Athens Archaeological Society from 1948 onward under Ioanna Papadimitriou, preserves the stoa and spring-house where the young arktoi served, along with vast deposits of votive offerings — miniature vessels, jewelry, and the garments dedicated by girls completing their service. Pausanias (1.33.1) saw Iphigéneia's tomb there and the clothes of women dead in childbirth dedicated at her shrine; Megara showed a rival tomb (1.43.1). At Aulis, excavation has identified the Classical temple terrace traditionally linked to the fleet's gathering, and at Chersonesos Taurica in Crimea the Greek city's remains long carried the later identification with her Taurian prison.
sources: Euripides, Iphigenia at Aulis; Iphigenia in Tauris
